# Generalised Linear Models (GLM)

In this file I will explore the abilities of Generalised Linear Models (GLM). In simple (or multivariate) linear regression, the inputs and outputs are both on a continuous scale, and their relationship are modelled as linear, meaning the expected output changes at a constant rate as the input changes, when other predictors are held constant. In generalised linear modelling, we give our inputs and outputs free reign, so that they can be non-continuous (and even categorical), while still imposing a linear relationship. The table below describes different types of models and their related inputs, outputs and response distribution. 

| Model | Input \(X\) | Output \(Y\) | Typical response distribution |
|-------|-------------|--------------|-------------------------------|
| Gaussian linear regression | Continuous or categorical | Continuous | Gaussian |
| Logistic regression | Continuous or categorical | Binary (0/1) | Bernoulli / Binomial |
| Poisson regression | Continuous or categorical | Discrete counts (0, 1, 2, …) | Poisson |
| Gamma regression | Continuous or categorical | Positive continuous | Gamma |

In order to apply linear modeling to data that is originally non-continuous, a link function connects the expected output to a linear model, allowing us to model outcomes such as binary values or counts. The link function transforms the conditional mean of the response variable onto a scale where it can be expressed as a linear function of the predictors.
